records.name_note: Admissible sources differ in how they present the common name. Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated single-species Plant Finder page has one Common Name line, and it reads 'smooth hydrangea.' NC State's dedicated species page instead carries a longer Common Name(s) list (Hills of Snow, Hortensia, Hydrangea, Sevenbark, Seven Bark, Smooth Hydrangea, Wild Hydrangea) rendered as seven separate list items in alphabetical order, and 'Smooth Hydrangea' appears in it. NC State's own species Description nonetheless leads with the name: 'Smooth hydrangea is a rounded, deciduous shrub in the hydrangea family (Hydrangeaceae).' RHS's dedicated page carries a different common name again, 'North American wild hydrangea', as its header subtitle. Because MoBot supplies a dedicated single-value field naming this exact taxon and NC State's own prose leads with the same name, 'Smooth Hydrangea' is used as the primary common name here. Distinct from Hydrangea quercifolia (Oakleaf Hydrangea) in this same batch and from the landed Bigleaf, Panicle and Climbing Hydrangeas.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox lists 'Poisonous' as one of four values of its Plant Type field under Whole Plant Traits (Native Plant, Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub) and, under its separate Problems field, tags this species 'Poisonous to Humans,' 'Problem for Cats,' 'Problem for Dogs,' and 'Problem for Horses.' This species' page carries no Poison Severity, Poison Symptoms, Poison Toxic Principle or Poison Part field and no severity banner, so no symptom list, severity rating or poison-part list can be reproduced from it. RHS's 'Potentially harmful' field for this species reads in full: 'Skin allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants.' Sources disagree on edibility scope: the same NC State page carries an Edibility field reading 'The Cherokee would eat the new growth of young twigs peeled, boiled or fried,' and a Uses (Ethnobotany) field recording Cherokee use of the plant as an emetic and antiseptic, with inner bark and leaves chewed as a stimulant. No admissible source names cyanogenic glycoside or any other toxic principle for this species, so that identification is not carried here.

No admissible source frames it as a houseplant or as a container subject.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's dedicated Taxus cuspidata page carries a human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans:' block. Poison Severity is 'High'. Poison Symptoms reads in full, both lines: 'Nervousness, trembling, slow pulse, pupil dilation, difficult breathing, seizures (dogs), abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, convulsions; may be fatal.' / 'Early signs: muscular tremors, dyspnea, seizures in dogs.' The Poison Part list is complete at all three values -- Bark, Leaves and Seeds -- and the page carries the standing line 'This plant has high severity poison characteristics.' The page's Problems field carries four independent tags -- 'Poisonous to Humans,' 'Problem for Cats,' 'Problem for Dogs,' and 'Problem for Horses' -- and the Whole Plant Traits block's Plant Type field lists 'Poisonous' alongside 'Shrub.' On edibility the sources disagree in scope: NC State's Fruit Description reads 'The red arils, in small amounts, are edible. The green seed is toxic.' and its Edibility field reads 'Bark, leaves, seed pit (red, fleshy surrounding part, called the aril, is OK to eat)', while RHS's Potentially harmful field gives a blanket warning with no aril carve-out: 'TOXIC if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. TOXIC to pets if eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers'. records.name_note: Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated single-species page carries one Common Name field for this taxon and it reads 'flowering quince', the form this record follows, title-cased. NC State's Common Name(s) list for the species leads with 'Common Flowering Quince' and gives 'Flowering Quince' second, and RHS's dedicated page renders 'Japanese quince' beneath its H1, so the sources split three ways on the lead. The name is genuinely shared: NC State's separate Chaenomeles japonica page lists 'Flowering quince' first among its own two common names, and NC State's C. speciosa page distinguishes the two by habit -- 'it is more upright than its relative Japanese flowering quince' -- the C. japonica page publishing 'Height: 2 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in.' against this species' 'Height: 6 ft. 0 in. - 12 ft. 0 in.' 'Flowering Quince' is the form most consistently used across the US admissible sources, so it is landed here with the ambiguity disclosed. Both RHS and MoBot list 'Cydonia speciosa' as a taxonomic synonym; that is a naming synonym, not the true quince Cydonia oblonga.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS's 'Potentially harmful' field for this species reads: 'Seeds contain toxins so these should be removed if you are considering eating the fruit; usually grown as an ornamental shrub. Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers'. The poison part named is the seeds; the 'Pets:' line is unscoped and names no specific animal, so it cannot support toxic_to_pets. All three sources nonetheless tag the fruit itself edible, and the disagreement is about preparation rather than about whether the plant is poisonous: NC State's Plant Type field carries 'Edible' (its two values are Edible and Shrub), its Uses (Ethnobotany) field reads 'Edible fruit, most often made into jam.', its Edibility field reads 'Used for making jellies and preserves', its Fruit Value To Gardener field reads 'Edible' and its tag list carries '#edible fruits'; MoBot's Fruit row reads 'Showy, Edible'; and RHS carries a rendered 'Fruit Edible' badge and the sentence 'These can be used to make jams and jellies but please see notes on toxicity for further advice'. None of them endorses eating the fruit raw: NC State's Description says 'These fruits are normally considered inedible right off of the tree due to their being hard and bitter; however, they are used to create preserves and jellies and some people eat them after having them set out to ripen,' and MoBot calls the fruit 'rather bitter when eaten fresh from the shrub, but quite tasty in preserves and jellies'. RHS alone flags the seed toxins. Handling: NC State's structured Problems field carries 'Spines/Thorns' and MoBot describes 'spiny, gray-brown twigs', so the shrub is armed.
